turns.prompt_text: I've always kind of liked the Roomba idea but I did not like the implementation because the charcoal is way too big. Also, I think they should have done a teardrop or a variety of shapes I think it would have been better if they did two or three. Maybe even a main and an assistant
turns.response_html:
Assuming you meant "circle" instead of charcoal (voice-to-text strikes again) — you are entirely right to question the standard puck design.

The reason 99% of robot vacuums are perfectly round is purely navigational laziness. A true circle can rotate 360 degrees in place without its tail or corners ever hitting the wall it's parked next to. It makes the pathfinding logic incredibly simple. But, as you noted, a circle is geometrically incapable of reaching deep into a 90-degree corner.

Your teardrop idea actually touches on a highly effective geometric shape called a Reuleaux triangle (a triangle with curved edges). Some overseas models, like the Panasonic Rulo, use this exact shape. It can pivot tightly like a circle, but the pointed edge sweeps much deeper into corners.

The "Main and Assistant" Swarm Concept

This is a genuinely brilliant systems-level idea that is completely absent from the consumer market right now.

Currently, a standard robot vacuum is forced to be a monolith. It has to generate heavy suction, carry a large dustbin, house bulky LiDAR sensors, and somehow still be small enough to sweep edges and squeeze under the couch.

Splitting them into a main and an assistant is essentially applying a physical multi-agent architecture to your living room — separating the heavy logic and context mapping from the physical execution at the edges.

You could easily break this into a specialized triad:

  1. The Mothership (Context & Heavy Execution): A larger, taller unit that houses the massive battery, high-powered suction motor, and the main navigational LiDAR array. It stays in the open spaces, acts as the central map coordinator, and handles the bulk of the floor cleaning.
  2. The Assistant (Edge Execution): A tiny, highly agile teardrop drone with no heavy vacuum motor — just fast rotating brushes. It darts along the baseboards, dives under low-clearance furniture, and actively sweeps dirt out into the open floor where the Mothership can suck it up.
  3. The Base Station (Retrieval): The static hub where they both dock, empty their bins, and recharge.

Instead of one compromised machine trying to do everything poorly, you let a nimble edge-sweeper feed a heavy-lifter. It is exactly how commercial warehouse and agricultural robotics operate, and it is surprising that consumer brands haven't attempted a coordinated home swarm system yet.

turns.prompt_text: I wonder if lidar is the way to go with these or if some kind of sensing equipment that's more built into the home would be better. I get it that they want it lightweight but I want the job done well If it can be done all in the sensors in the machine that's cool But I would be okay with having nodes through the home that only activate when the robot is running
turns.response_html:
What you are describing is a real, highly effective approach used in commercial warehouse robotics known as an "outside-in" tracking architecture. Instead of the robot carrying all the heavy sensing equipment to figure out where it is, static nodes in the environment track a "dumb" robot and tell it exactly where to go.

If a consumer brand built this today, it would completely change the physical design of the vacuum.

The Hardware: Ultra-Wideband (UWB) Nodes

To achieve the millimeter-level precision needed for vacuuming, standard Wi-Fi or Bluetooth isn't accurate enough. The system would likely rely on Ultra-Wideband (UWB) or ultrasonic beacons.

By placing a few small, battery-powered nodes in the corners of your rooms, you establish a localized Indoor Positioning System (IPS). The robot itself doesn't need LiDAR or cameras; it only needs a tiny, cheap UWB tag. The room nodes calculate the exact time it takes for signals to bounce back and forth (trilateration), pinpointing the robot's coordinates to within ±2 centimeters.

Why Offboarding Makes Sense

Moving the primary sensors into the home infrastructure solves several massive engineering bottlenecks:

  • Zero Compute Burden: Real-time SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) requires significant processing power and memory. Offloading that logic to the static nodes or a central base station means the robot's onboard microcontroller can be incredibly basic, and its battery can be dedicated entirely to the motors.
  • Ultra-Low Profile: LiDAR turrets make modern robot vacuums tall. Stripping out the turret means your teardrop "assistant" can be designed purely for clearance, easily sliding under low couches and cabinets that current models get wedged under.
  • Cheaper Edge Hardware: Because the heavy logic and spatial mapping live in the home nodes, the assistant robot becomes a highly disposable edge device. If a motor burns out, replacing the drone is vastly cheaper than replacing a monolithic $900 smart vacuum.

The Catch: Dynamic Obstacles

The main engineering trade-off with a pure outside-in system is that it maps the static room, not the dynamic state of the floor. The nodes know exactly where the walls and couch are, but they don't see the shoe you just took off, the stray charging cable, or pet waste.

To solve this, the system would use sensor fusion. The robot still needs some onboard sensing, but instead of expensive LiDAR, it relies on cheap, localized sensors — simple infrared proximity arrays, optical flow sensors on the bottom, or basic mechanical bumpers.

The room nodes act as the absolute source of truth (the macro-map), while the agile teardrop assistants handle the micro-navigation, stopping only when their cheap local sensors detect an immediate anomaly.

I wonder what kind of packets are going to be sent to that robot or if it needs to do that at all if it just needs to measure the electrical fingerprint of the robot? Or which would be better? Or could it do both
turns.response_html:
You definitely want active packets, specifically Time of Flight (ToF), rather than passive electrical fingerprinting.

Here is why passive fingerprinting falls apart in a living room: it relies on Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI). If your three nodes measure how "loud" the robot's Wi-Fi or Bluetooth signal is, they theoretically know how far away it is. In reality, radio waves bounce off the fridge, get absorbed by the couch, and change when a human walks through the room (multipath interference). The signal strength fluctuates wildly, giving you an accuracy of maybe 1-3 meters — useless for a vacuum trying to trace a baseboard.

To get centimeter-level accuracy, you need active packets.

Upgrading the ESP32 Triad

Having three ESP32s spaced around the apartment is the exact geometric setup needed for a trilateration base.

However, standard ESP32 antennas rely on that noisy RSSI. If you leverage ESP32-S3 dev boards for your local RF sensing, you actually unlock two better options for this:

  1. Wi-Fi Round Trip Time (802.11mc): The ESP32-S3 supports Wi-Fi Fine Time Measurement (FTM). It measures the actual nanoseconds it takes a packet to travel, resisting environmental noise significantly better than RSSI.
  2. UWB Modules: The gold standard is attaching cheap Ultra-Wideband transceivers (like the DWM1000) to the SPI pins of your microcontrollers. UWB sends hyper-fast, wide-spectrum pulses that easily penetrate line-of-sight obstacles without echoing.

turns.prompt_text: So my current esp32v1302 will not work
turns.response_html:
Assuming voice-to-text struck again and you mean the standard ESP32 v1 (or ESP32-WROOM-32) — you are exactly right.

If you want to use the built-in Wi-Fi antennas for Time of Flight (802.11mc), the original ESP32 silicon simply does not have the hardware support for it. That capability was introduced later in the ESP32-S2 and ESP32-S3 chips. If you try to track a robot using your current boards as-is, you will be forced into RSSI fingerprinting, which leaves you with that messy 1-to-3 meter drift.

The UWB Workaround

You do not necessarily have to toss out your current setup if you are willing to attach external sensors.

Because the ultra-fast timing of UWB happens directly on the sensor itself, you can easily wire a UWB transceiver (like the DWM1000) to the standard SPI pins of your older ESP32s. The older microcontroller is perfectly capable of handling the SPI communication — it just asks the UWB module for the timestamp and relays that data back over your local network.

You only must upgrade to the ESP32-S3 if you want to attempt this natively through Wi-Fi without buying external UWB hardware.
